mcqs.question: What does the weak generational hypothesis claim, and why does it justify a generational collector's design?
options: That all objects live exactly as long as the program runs
That objects are freed in the same order they were allocated
That memory usage grows linearly with program runtime
That most objects die shortly after allocation, so tracing just the recently-allocated region finds most of the garbage cheaply
mcqs.explanation: The hypothesis is specifically about lifetime skew — most allocations are short-lived — which is why a small young generation catches most garbage without scanning the whole heap. It says nothing about allocation/free ordering or linear memory growth, and it's explicitly not a claim that objects live forever.

mcqs.question: Why does a generational collector need a write barrier at all, given that a minor GC only needs to trace the young generation?
options: To make heap allocation itself faster by pre-zeroing memory
To compress old-generation objects and save space
To let the minor GC run on a background thread automatically
To record when an old-generation object gains a pointer into the young generation, so the minor GC doesn't miss that the young object is reachable
mcqs.explanation: Without recording cross-generational pointers, a minor GC that only traces roots plus the young generation could miss that an old object references a young one, and incorrectly free something still live. Write barriers exist to catch exactly that case; they don't affect allocation speed, compression, or threading by themselves.

mcqs.question: A service reports p99 latency spikes matching 200ms GC pauses. Based on the young/old generation cost model, which is the more likely source?
options: Minor GCs, since they run more frequently
Major/full GCs, since their cost scales with the size of the old generation's live set
Both generations contribute equally regardless of size
Neither — write barrier overhead alone can't cause multi-hundred-millisecond pauses
mcqs.explanation: Minor GCs are bounded by the deliberately small young generation and typically run in single-digit milliseconds; a 200ms pause is squarely in major-GC territory, where the cost scales with however much long-lived data the old generation actually holds. Write barrier overhead is spread continuously and isn't the source of a discrete large pause.

mcqs.question: A concurrent collector traces the object graph while the mutator keeps running. What correctness problem does this reintroduce that stop-the-world collection avoided by brute force?
options: The mutator could mutate the pointer graph mid-trace, letting a live object slip past detection unless the collector has extra bookkeeping to catch it
The heap could run out of address space during tracing
Multiple threads could allocate objects with the same address
The mark phase would no longer be a graph traversal
mcqs.explanation: Stop-the-world sidesteps mutation-during-trace by freezing the mutator entirely; letting the mutator keep running reopens exactly that risk, which is why concurrent collectors add tricolor marking and write barriers specifically to catch a mutator write that would otherwise hide a live reference from the tracer. It's unrelated to address space exhaustion, address collisions, or the traversal algorithm itself.

mcqs.question: A cache with high churn keeps getting promoted to the old generation before its entries are evicted, and GC pause times get worse. What's this failure mode called, and why does it hurt?
options: Write barrier saturation — every cache write triggers a barrier check that overwhelms the collector
Premature promotion — short-lived-in-spirit objects end up in the old generation, defeating the young generation's job of catching most garbage cheaply
Heap fragmentation — the cache's varying entry sizes leave unusable gaps
Reference cycle formation — cache entries referencing each other block collection
mcqs.explanation: The cache's high churn means entries survive long enough (relative to minor GC frequency) to get promoted, landing objects that are really short-lived into the region the collector scans rarely and expensively — the exact inversion of the generational hypothesis the design assumes. Write barrier cost, fragmentation, and cycles are all real GC-related issues, just not the one described here.

mcqs.question: Before touching any GC tuning flags to fix 200ms p99 pauses, what should you check first?
options: Whether increasing the young generation size alone fixes it, without checking anything else
GC logs — pause type, old-generation occupancy trend, and promotion rate — to identify whether this is a growing live set, premature promotion, or an algorithmic mismatch
Whether switching languages entirely would remove the problem
The application's unit test coverage percentage
mcqs.explanation: Every credible diagnosis path starts with measurement — GC logs show pause type directly, and occupancy/promotion trends distinguish a real leak, premature promotion, or a collector simply mismatched to the live-set size, each of which needs a different fix. Guessing at a single tuning flag, switching languages, or checking test coverage don't diagnose the actual cause.
